html:
Chavín was a culture of the northern highlands of Peru, centred on the temple of Chavín de Huántar, from about 900 to 200 BCE. Its religious art spread over much of Peru, so archaeologists call its time the Early Horizon, the first period when one style united a large part of the Andes.

The temple stands at about 3,150 m where two rivers meet, on a route between the coast and the Amazon. Inside are dark stone passages. In the centre stands the Lanzón, a tall carved stone showing a fanged god. Channels carried water under the temple, perhaps to make roaring sounds, and conch-shell trumpets have been found there. Carved stone heads once looked out from the walls.

Its art mixes jaguars, eagles, caimans and snakes, many of them animals of the Amazon lowlands. Carvings show a cactus with mind-altering effects, which priests may have used in rituals.

Chavín style turns up far away on pottery, textiles and gold, for example on the south coast, where it influenced Paracas. Chavín drew on older coastal centres such as Caral and El Paraíso. After it faded, regional cultures rose, among them the Moche and the Nazca. The temple is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
